diagnosis: The left panel shows over 1,100 pairs with slack below \(10^{-15}\), essentially machine precision, while the configuration has only about \(184\cdot7-28=1{,}260\) effective tangential degrees of freedom, so the LP-polished solution is jammed at an almost isostatic, highly degenerate vertex with no useful linearized descent direction. The contact graph is also extremely unbalanced, ranging from 0 to roughly 28 contacts per point, with one rattler and a conspicuous low-contact block around indices 85–105; thus the load is carried by a subset of points while other degrees of freedom are wasted. The best solution therefore lacks a balanced, equi-tight, positive-stress contact structure—and apparently any organizing symmetry or algebraic structure—that a substantially better optimum might possess. Small perturbations followed by softmax annealing predictably slide back into the same basin, explaining why the leading programs have identical scores, while repeated expensive LP calls explain the timeouts.

diagnosis: The image shows at least ~1,100 pairs with slack below $10^{-15}$, so the incumbent is LP-polished to machine precision and completely jammed. Against only $184\cdot7-28=1260$ effective tangent degrees of freedom this leaves almost no feasible first-order motion, yet the contact load is badly unbalanced: one rattler has 0 contacts, a block around indices 75–110 has only 2–12, and several hubs have 26–29. Small shakes, single-rattler relocations, and softmax reconvergence therefore slide back into the same contact topology, while repeated LP calls inside hopping loops explain the many timeouts. Structurally, the missing property is a balanced, fully participating, near-isostatic contact network—every point should carry a comparable, moderate number of contacts and there is no evident symmetric/algebraic regularity in the projected contact graph to exploit for a collective escape.

diagnosis: The best configuration is severely LP-jammed: over 1100 pairs lie within about \(10^{-15}\) of the maximum cosine, so the linearized LP has essentially no useful descent direction and merely tightens the same active face. It is nevertheless structurally unbalanced—one point is a rattler with zero contacts while others have up to 29—so it lacks an equi-contact, load-balanced tight configuration in which every point helps constrain the optimum. Nearly all successful programs start from `best.npy`, apply small or rattler-only perturbations, and then monotonically reconverge to exactly \(0.4999829530317\), indicating that the contact graph, inherited from the near-\(0.5\) record/E8-like structure, never changes. Larger basin-hopping attempts often exceed the time limit before producing a polished alternative. Progress therefore requires new topologies or symmetry classes, not more polishing of this jammed optimum.
